body.objective: Students will be able to use tools safely.
successCriteria: I can identify common hand tools and their uses
I can follow safety rules for tools and the workshop

body.hook: Every year, workplace injuries send thousands of Canadian workers to hospital, and many happen with simple hand tools. Professionals in trades don't avoid tools; they respect them. Safety is the first skill of every builder.

study.title: Tool Licence
study.question: How do I use tools safely in the workshop?
study.passage:
Workshop safety rules (written for this lesson):
1. Wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling, sanding or hammering. Tie back long hair and remove dangling items.
2. Only use a tool after the teacher has demonstrated it and you have passed the tool check.
3. Clamp your work. Never hold small pieces in your hand while cutting or drilling.
4. Cut away from your body and keep your other hand behind the blade.
5. Carry tools pointed down; never run in the workshop.
6. Report broken tools and injuries right away.
7. Clean up: return tools to their place and sweep sawdust.
Common tools: tape measure and steel rule (measuring), try square (marking right angles), coping saw and tenon saw (cutting), hand drill (making holes), clamps and vise (holding), sandpaper and files (smoothing), screwdriver and hammer (joining).
Tool check: At each station, name the tool, its use and one safety rule, then demonstrate holding it correctly.

body.objective: Students will be able to build a prototype.
successCriteria: I can explain what a prototype is and why it is made
I can build a prototype from my design drawing
I can record changes I make while building
body.hook: Engineers build cardboard and foam models of cars and planes before spending millions on the real thing. A prototype is a test version: cheap, quick and meant to teach you something. Today you build yours.

vocabulary.definition: An early model built to test a design.
A representation of a design, sometimes at a smaller scale.
The ratio between the size of a model and the real object.
A record of what you did, problems and changes while building.
A change made to a design.
A quick, rough prototype, often in card, to check size and shape.

study.title: Build Day
study.question: How does building a prototype test my design?
study.passage:
Build plan (written for this lesson):
Stage 1, Mock-up (one lesson): Build a full-size mock-up of your desk organizer in card and tape. Place real pencils, a 30 cm ruler, a phone and sticky notes in it. Do they fit? Is it stable?
Stage 2, Modify: Mark any changes on your orthographic drawing in a different colour.
Stage 3, Prototype (two lessons): Build the organizer in your chosen material using safe tool techniques. Follow the order: measure and mark, cut, smooth, test-fit, join, finish.
Build log: After each lesson write the date, what you did, one problem and how you solved it, and any change to the design.
Example log entry: "Day 2. Cut base and two sides. The phone slot was 8 mm too narrow in the mock-up, so I widened it to 18 mm on the drawing before cutting."

body.objective: Students will be able to use measuring and joining techniques.
body.iCan: I can use measuring and joining techniques.
successCriteria: I can measure and mark accurately
I can choose a suitable joining method
I can explain tolerance and why accuracy matters
body.hook: "Measure twice, cut once" is one of the oldest sayings in carpentry. A cut 3 mm too short can't be uncut. And a joint that wobbles makes the whole product weak. Today you sharpen two core building skills: measuring and joining.

vocabulary.definition: The amount a measurement can be off and still work, such as ± 1 mm.
Two pieces joined end to face, usually with glue, nails or screws.
A line where two pieces of fabric are sewn together.
The fabric between the edge and the stitching line, often 1.5 cm.
The width of material removed by a saw blade.

study.title: Precision Challenge
study.question: How do accurate measuring and strong joining make a better product?
study.passage:
Precision stations (written for this lesson):
Station 1, Measure and mark: Mark three cuts at 87 mm, 142 mm and 205 mm on a strip using a steel rule and a sharp pencil. Your partner checks each mark. Tolerance: ± 1 mm.
Station 2, Kerf: Cut on the waste side of the line. A saw blade removes about 1 to 2 mm; if you cut on the line, your piece will be too short.
Station 3, Joining methods: Compare a glued butt joint, a nailed butt joint, a screwed joint and a dowel joint. Hang a 1 kg mass from each after the glue dries. Which holds best? Which looks best?
Station 4, Textile joining: Sew a straight seam with a 1.5 cm seam allowance by hand or machine. Check it is straight and the stitches are even.
Choosing a joint: Consider strength, appearance, tools available, time and whether the product must come apart.
